name: Aquamarine
lede: Aquamarine is the pale blue-green of the gem beryl and the sea, and a web color whose screen version is far brighter than the stone.

sections.title: Sea water and sailors
sections.body:
Aquamarine is a name for seawater. Finlay explains that the gem was named for the color of clear, deep salt water, and that the stones were believed lucky for sailors, who in classical times often wore them to appease the sea-god Poseidon [1]. Paterson defines the color word as a pale bluish green, a sea-color [2].

In the gem, color is a matter of a trace metal. Finlay explains that beryl with chromium grows into [[emerald]], while beryl with iron grows into the pale blue stones called aquamarine, which she calls emerald's sisters [1]. She mentions Cleopatra's mines, which she ties to aquamarine rather than emerald, as a thought experiment about what iron in place of chromium would have meant [1].

sections.title: In old lists
sections.body:
A passage in Pliny's *Natural History* (book 37, ch. 16) about looking through an emerald is read by some scholars as aquamarine, because emerald is usually too dark to see through [3]. Pastoureau notes that the twelve stones of the high priest's breastplate in Exodus include a stone now translated as aquamarine, but the names are hard to match to colors and the translations are uncertain [4]. Paterson's modern list of birthstones gives March as aquamarine or bloodstone and pale blue as its color, and warns that the lists are an amalgam of many [2].

In the color library, Maerz and Paul (1930) give the first recorded use of the word as 1598 [5]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it under several blocks [5]. In painting, Ball uses the word for the blue-green set against red in Raphael's *Madonna del Granduca* of about 1505 [6].

sections.title: The web color
sections.body: Paterson lists Aquamarine among the 140 colors of the X11 set, with hex code 7FFFD4 [2]. That is a very light, fully saturated mint-cyan [5]. Real aquamarines are paler and bluer, and vary stone to stone [1][2]. If you see the gem, expect a cooler, calmer color than the swatch.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this exact color covering as much as one per cent of the canvas, within a color distance of 4 [7]. That says something about the screen color, not about painting: it is brighter than any varnished pigment [7]. The match is as photographed [7].

The word is another story. In Google Books, *aquamarine* first rises above a rounding error around 1860, climbs from the 1940s, and peaks around 2010 [7]. The color has been spreading as a word for decades [7].

questions.q: What turns beryl into aquamarine rather than emerald?
Real aquamarine gems are usually brighter and more saturated than the web swatch.

openers: The gem aquamarine and emerald are the same mineral, beryl; iron makes the first, chromium the second [1].

issues: Finlay says the stones were believed lucky for sailors; 'safer' reworded to match
